\{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ y={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.54$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.54$ | $0.59$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/30/30d1e296e7c83fa8925feb116c9035de14790e89ddad37ab44710feacadf13a8.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)|\le 1,$ $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)|\le 1,$ and ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, the curve $\text{converges}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we have $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

Again, since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

{{field-6}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that the given curve is $\text{bounded}$ (and closed), representing $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

But we have that:

- ${e}^{at}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty $ when $a>0,$ and

- ${e}^{at}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty $ when $a<0.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=2>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$

"f6c8c4d4-3353-5b89-8ca9-42cba1be9033" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "an unstable spiral (source)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168010 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+\frac{1}{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
![](images/d1/d13abb97b171049a17544fcb312b71d2da3d9294788c1aebe7aa969e99b7819c.svg)
we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ y={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4f/4f9da4b66977b98b983477d22abb6e00135ea0e1bfa9f785cd0a62d674a7b782.png)

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/62/62380812d6fbe4e28531a455814296a4969a0744fb28a94a5e2d7c588ec5cfc4.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168025 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a linear system
![](images/65/6597a81f818926afff9056180de0e12357ef7631be093aba32626a7461079c18.svg)
where the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ are

$$
\lambda_{1,2}=a\pm bi,
\qquad b\neq 0.
$$

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- The type of the curve is determined by the parameter $a{:}$

- If $a=0,$ we have bounded closed curves (ellipses/circles).

- If $a \neq 0,$ we have spirals.

- The stability is determined by the sign of $a{:}$

- If $a>0,$ we have an **unstable spiral** (source).

- If $a<0,$ we have a **stable spiral** (sink).

- If $a=0,$ we have a **center**.

**Note:** The center is a *stable* equilibrium but not *asymptotically stable* since trajectories do not converge to it.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167012 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

{{field-6}}." :question/worked-solution "Let $v=p+q\text{i},$ where $p,q\in {R}^{2},$ be an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =a+b\text{i}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that the given curve is $\text{bounded}$ (and closed), representing $\text{an ellipse}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

But we have that:

- ${e}^{at}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty $ when $a>0,$ and

- ${e}^{at}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty $ when $a<0.$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=2>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{2t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$

"f6c8c4d4-3353-5b89-8ca9-42cba1be9033" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "an unstable spiral (source)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168010 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-4y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4x(t)+\frac{1}{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
![](images/d1/d13abb97b171049a17544fcb312b71d2da3d9294788c1aebe7aa969e99b7819c.svg)
we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ y={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4f/4f9da4b66977b98b983477d22abb6e00135ea0e1bfa9f785cd0a62d674a7b782.png)

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/62/62380812d6fbe4e28531a455814296a4969a0744fb28a94a5e2d7c588ec5cfc4.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186168025 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a linear system
![](images/65/6597a81f818926afff9056180de0e12357ef7631be093aba32626a7461079c18.svg)
where the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ are

$$
\lambda_{1,2}=a\pm bi,
\qquad b\neq 0.
$$

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- The type of the curve is determined by the parameter $a{:}$

- If $a=0,$ we have bounded closed curves (ellipses/circles).

- If $a \neq 0,$ we have spirals.

- The stability is determined by the sign of $a{:}$

- If $a>0,$ we have an **unstable spiral** (source).

- If $a<0,$ we have a **stable spiral** (sink).

- If $a=0,$ we have a **center**.

**Note:** The center is a *stable* equilibrium but not *asymptotically stable* since trajectories do not converge to it.

Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167012 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186166550 :question/problem "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

![](images/07/07d13106e7599d36636da2101ac0bc8fb73b26062416f915a0253097eb85108c.png)"] ["question-99d67f71-7edc-5901-bbd8-911b5a0d051c" :question/worked-solution "The general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]={c}_{1}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}],\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ y={e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{8}$ | $\frac{\pi }{4}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $1.05$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $1.05$ | $2.19$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4b/4bcb5580c38573cfdd9839a9d305deec877945a2206aea7db6d69ec37d20ee33.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)|\le 1$ and $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)|\le 1$ but ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, the curve $\text{diverges}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we have $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

Again, since ${e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}$ as $t\to \infty .$

The $\text{phase portrait}$ of our system looks as follows:

For example, when ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=0,$ we obtain the following curve:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ y={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\frac{\pi }{12}$ | $\frac{\pi }{6}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.54$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.54$ | $0.59$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/30/30d1e296e7c83fa8925feb116c9035de14790e89ddad37ab44710feacadf13a8.png)

Notice that $|\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)|\le 1,$ $|\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)|\le 1,$ and ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, the curve $\text{converges}$ as $t\to \infty .$ So, we have $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$

Again, since ${e}^{-t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ the spiral is traversed toward $\text{the origin}$ as $t\to \infty .$

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is $\text{unbounded},$ representing $\text{a spiral}$ that is traversed $\text{counterclockwise}.$ Thus, we must have $a\ne 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward $\text{infinity}.$

Hence, to insure that ${e}^{at}\to \infty ,$ we require $a>0.$"] ["question-7f3e4a87-6028-52e9-bf97-2ee9eb5bc473" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] $$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=3>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) = \mathbf{v} e^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\textbf{x}(t) = 
c_1 e^{at}\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big) + 
c_2 e^{at}\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big),
$$

where the parts $\big(\cos(bt)\mathbf{p}-\sin(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ and $\big(\sin(bt)\mathbf{p}+\cos(bt)\mathbf{q}\big)$ are bounded.

Now notice that the given curve is unbounded, representing a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise. Thus, we must have $a \neq 0.$

Also, notice that the spiral is traversed toward the origin.

Hence, to insure that $e^{at} \to 0,$ we require $a < 0.$"} {:db/id 17592186048535} {:db/id 17592186167229 :question/id #uuid "0d2fdbc8-ed30-59a9-869b-569e3f094dfe" :question/math-academy-id Then, a complex solution of the system is given by

$$
{x}_{\text{complex}}(t)=v{e}^{\lambda t}.
$$

Using Euler's formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{complex}}(t) & =v{e}^{(a+b\text{i})t} \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt))(p+q\text{i}) \\  & ={e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+\text{i}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution of the system is

$$
\text{x}(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)+{c}_{2}{e}^{at}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q),
$$

where the parts $(\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)p-\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)q)$ and $(\operatorname{sin}⁡(bt)p+\operatorname{cos}⁡(bt)q)$ are bounded.

Now, notice that $a=\text{Re}(\lambda )=1>0$ and ${e}^{at}={e}^{t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty .$ Thus, we have a spiral that is traversed toward infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Let's see some concrete examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "2a925aab-4f30-57a3-a3a2-6c3e21b5b318" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14482 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b0e4834-5b7b-5ae6-a7c1-b1def5543b1d" :step/math-academy-id 594290 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167905}} {:db/id 17592186167905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168010 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-4y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=4x(t)+\frac{1}{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}(4t) \\ y={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4f/4f9da4b66977b98b983477d22abb6e00135ea0e1bfa9f785cd0a62d674a7b782.png)

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/62/62380812d6fbe4e28531a455814296a4969a0744fb28a94a5e2d7c588ec5cfc4.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f3d4213d-a0e4-5bda-9e29-8eca4801de63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14483 :tutorial/title "Systems With Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "89ecb234-3886-5849-970a-abafcfaa1df5" :step/math-academy-id 594291 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167906}} {:db/id 17592186167906 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166941 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166550 :question/id #uuid "8337af7a-73e8-5ae2-9bed-b03f193b2950" :question/math-academy-id "e-21657"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "113b981d-bbf2-588a-be74-028506cdb19d" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048395} {:db/id 17592186048992} {:db/id 17592186049672} {:db/id 17592186050309}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167223} {:db/id 17592186167224} {:db/id 17592186308498} {:db/id 17592186308501}] :knowledge-point/title "Sketching the Phase Portrait of a System"} :step/id #uuid "94fe1e57-9c9a-561e-bfd5-2ae1e6a4369a" :step/math-academy-id 594292 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167907}} {:db/id 17592186167907 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166942 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166551 :question/id #uuid "7b4f569b-ad3a-5a93-a53e-27a186b7700e" :question/math-academy-id "e-21658"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b542bd66-f4f8-5b4e-a3e7-4717827c427a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048535}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167229} {:db/id 17592186167242} {:db/id 17592186308591} {:db/id 17592186308592} {:db/id 17592186385185} {:db/id 17592186391460}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Parameters of a System Given Its Phase Portrait"} :step/id #uuid "6468cc1a-a1a6-502b-82f1-16821ba5d8c4" :step/math-academy-id 594295 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167908}} {:db/id 17592186167908 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168025 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

Again, we are considering a linear system

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

where the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ are

$$
\lambda_{1,2}=a\pm bi,
\qquad b\neq 0.
$$

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- The type of the curve is determined by the parameter $a{:}$

- If $a=0,$ we have bounded closed curves (ellipses/circles).

- If $a \neq 0,$ we have spirals.

- The stability is determined by the sign of $a{:}$

- If $a>0,$ we have an **unstable spiral** (source).

- If $a<0,$ we have a **stable spiral** (sink).

- If $a=0,$ we have a **center**.

**Note:** The center is a *stable* equilibrium but not *asymptotically stable* since trajectories do not converge to it.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c36d256f-edd3-5079-9f72-da6e3a8b4f91" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14575 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "6209ec28-abe9-501f-8925-5c8a06aee7df" :step/math-academy-id 594299 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167909}} {:db/id 17592186167909 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166943 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166552 :question/id #uuid "d7b40689-7b7e-546e-9b66-30e6a95f3ee0" :question/math-academy-id "e-21659"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9f0b176c-c802-5b3b-85d0-dede602c9bf3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048990}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167230} {:db/id 17592186167243} {:db/id 17592186308593} {:db/id 17592186308594} {:db/id 17592186308595} {:db/id 17592186308596} {:db/id 17592186308597} {:db/id 17592186308598}] :knowledge-point/title "Classifying Systems of Linear Differential Equations With Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "4d18ae8d-2ebf-569f-bebb-2a856d39ef9d" :step/math-academy-id 594300}] :activity/title "Phase Portraits for Linear Systems With Complex Eigenvalues" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186167012} {:db/id 17592186167904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168009 :tutorial/content "In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{'}(t)=\frac{1}{2}x(t)-4y(t) \\ {y}^{'}(t)=4x(t)+\frac{1}{2}y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}(4t) \\ y={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Let's sketch this solution in the phase space.

![](images/4f/4f9da4b66977b98b983477d22abb6e00135ea0e1bfa9f785cd0a62d674a7b782.png)

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$

The phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

![](images/62/62380812d6fbe4e28531a455814296a4969a0744fb28a94a5e2d7c588ec5cfc4.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f3d4213d-a0e4-5bda-9e29-8eca4801de63" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14483 :tutorial/title "Systems With Complex Eigenvalues"} :step/id #uuid "89ecb234-3886-5849-970a-abafcfaa1df5" :step/math-academy-id 594291 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167906}} {:db/id 17592186168010 :tutorial/content "Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

Again, we are considering a linear system

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

where the eigenvalues of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ are

$$
\lambda_{1,2}=a\pm bi,
\qquad b\neq 0.
$$

As for the classification of the equilibrium at the origin, we get the following:

- The type of the curve is determined by the parameter $a{:}$

- If $a=0,$ we have bounded closed curves (ellipses/circles).

- If $a \neq 0,$ we have spirals.

- The stability is determined by the sign of $a{:}$

- If $a>0,$ we have an **unstable spiral** (source).

- If $a<0,$ we have a **stable spiral** (sink).

- If $a=0,$ we have a **center**.

**Note:** The center is a *stable* equilibrium but not *asymptotically stable* since trajectories do not converge to it.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "c36d256f-edd3-5079-9f72-da6e3a8b4f91" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14575 :tutorial/title "Classification of Equilibria"} :step/id #uuid "6209ec28-abe9-501f-8925-5c8a06aee7df" :step/math-academy-id 594299 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167909}} {:db/id 17592186168025 :tutorial/content "Finally, let’s summarize what we’ve learned so far.

These tools provide the mathematical foundation for analyzing electromagnetic fields, wave phenomena, dynamical systems, and statistical models encountered in advanced physics courses." 17592186045417] [17592186046660 1009 "The course begins with the theory of projections in inner product spaces. Students study norms, inner products, orthogonality, and orthogonal complements in vector spaces over the real and complex numbers. Techniques such as orthogonal projections, the Gram–Schmidt process, and QR factorization allow vectors to be decomposed into orthogonal components. These ideas play a role in Fourier analysis, signal decomposition, and numerical methods used in physical simulations.
Students then explore quadratic forms and the diagonalization of symmetric matrices. The spectral theorem provides a geometric interpretation of symmetric transformations and leads to techniques for analyzing energy functions and stability in physical systems. Singular value decomposition is also introduced as a powerful matrix factorization with applications in numerical modeling and data analysis.
Applications of linear algebra follow, including least-squares methods for solving overdetermined systems. These methods arise when fitting theoretical models to experimental data and when approximating solutions to physical equations.
The course then develops multivariable integration in three dimensions. Students compute triple integrals over general regions and apply coordinate transformations such as cylindrical and spherical coordinates. These techniques allow physicists to compute quantities such as mass distributions, charge densities, and gravitational or electric potentials.
Students next study line integrals and surface integrals of scalar and vector fields. Concepts such as circulation, flux, and path independence lead to the fundamental theorems of vector calculus, including Green’s theorem, the divergence theorem, and Stokes’ theorem. These results form the mathematical framework underlying conservation laws and the differential and integral formulations of electromagnetic theory.
Applications of multivariable calculus follow, including vector mechanics and optimization. Students analyze motion using vector-valued functions, apply Newton’s second law to systems in the plane, and study work–energy relationships. Multiple integrals are used to compute mass, centers of mass, moments of inertia, and other physical quantities.
The course then returns to differential equations, extending earlier techniques to systems of linear differential equations. Students analyze dynamical systems using eigenvalues, phase portraits, and matrix methods, which appear in models of interacting systems such as coupled oscillators or predator–prey dynamics.
Laplace transforms are introduced as a powerful tool for solving linear differential equations with discontinuous inputs or initial conditions. Boundary value problems and Fourier series are then developed, providing mathematical techniques used to solve differential equations describing heat flow, vibrating strings, wave propagation, and other physical phenomena.
The course concludes with numerical methods for differential equations and advanced probability topics. The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\pm4\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 1]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is

$$
[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]
$$

we are interested in sketching the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.

If we set $c_1 = 1$ and $c_2 = 0$ in the general solution of the system, we obtain the particular solution:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{cos}(4t) \\ y={e}^{t/2}\operatorname{sin}(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

| $t$ | $0$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{16}$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $x$ | $1$ | $0.78$ | $0$ |
| $y$ | $0$ | $0.78$ | $1.22$ |

Notice that $|\sin(4t)| \leq 1$ and $|\cos(4t)| \leq 1,$ but $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty.$ Thus, the obtained curve is unbounded. So, we have a spiral that is traversed counterclockwise.

Again, since $e^{t/2} \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty,$ the spiral is traversed toward infinity as $t \to \infty.$
